Hey folks, so SSDs have become pervasive and cheap in the industry, and everybody's got one! I also work for a company that handles literally hundreds of 240, 512 and 1024 GB SSDs per week. Most of those SSDs come across my desk for testing/verification etc. I only started working there last year but they have been doing the SSD dance for about 4 years now.

Our main concerns are reliability, degradation rate and DOA rate. These drives have to be deployed for years at a time and some of them have been in the field for 4 years now. We have found a few things out. You pay for quality and some drives are not worth the metal they are housed in. They abandoned all OCZ products before I even got their. We have had nothing but problems with the Samsung EVO 840. Kingston and Corsair are also no good.

These are the brands and products I recommend based on my experience: 1: Intel 320, 520, and 730 Series 2: SanDisk ExtremPro (or better) 3: Samsung 850 Pro. Intel despite a few firmware issues a while ago is as solid as a rock. Ridiculously good in all 3 categories. SanDisk ExtremePro is near Intel in terms of reliability and really, really fast. Their drives do everything fast, including hot-swapping on/off the system. Samsung 850 Pro is acceptable, they have pretty good reliability, they make some of the largest drives and they are decently fast. They take forever to mount and unmount, like 30 seconds sometimes, it's pretty irritating. My personal drive is 4 years old and has had issues for the last 2, it's a Corsair Force GS from mid 2011 (not 100% on the year, I built this rig in 2011 but I forget exactly when I threw in the SSD) and I would nominally give it a pretty garbage rating.

ITT Post your experiences with SSDs and discuss their merits and draw backs! My personal opinion is pretty clear: Intel has all around the best product, I'm about to put a 240GB 730 in my new build!

EDIT: Woah! I'm at work, I'll sift through this when I get home!

edit: Samsung EVO and PRO are different brands, oops! also line breaks

Well shit...I have a Samsung 840 EVO. What kind of issues did you experience and how long would you expect it to last before degradation? I've had it for about 7 months now and have not experienced any issues so far.

We almost used the 840, but it does have some problems. So far they have been fine as far as degradation and failure rate, no red flags there but long-term reliability is low. But Samsung had all sorts of firmware issues, the drives first slowed down to ~80MB/s read/write (so check your speeds), Samsung put out that 'Performance restoration' program to fix the issue but required us to wipe all extant drives. We use them as 1TB data drives and they take so long to initialize that the system is booted and our program fails to launch because it cannot find the data drive yet. They also have a firmware issue that causes it to sometimes fail to initialize at all. This is an enterprise application where we may not see the drive at all for the next 4 years or something so we have to be pretty strict on these things. Samsung was marginally helpful in fixing the issues but not really.

I think a more important metric would be "If a human was driving the car, would there have been an accident?". Even though a human is "at fault" in some cases the car could have avoided the accident. For example, from the report linked from the article we have this:

A Google Lexus model AV was travelling northbound on El Camino Real in autonomous mode when another vehicle traveling westbound on View Street failed to come to a stop at the stop sign at the intersection of El Camino and View Street. The other vehicle rolled through the stop sign and struck the right rear quarter panel and right rear wheel of the Google AV. Prior to the collision, the Google AV’s autonomous technology began applying the brakes in response to its detection of the other vehicle’s speed and trajectory. Just before the collision, the driver of the Google AV disengaged autonomous mode and took manual control of the vehicle in response to the application of the brakes

In this case, the other car rolled through the stop sign after the google car was in the intersection. The car's response was to slam on its brakes which caused the google car to get hit in the rear end. If a human was in control, this accident would not have happened. Yes, the other driver was legally at fault, but the accident was actually caused by the autonomous car.

Looking at the report there were 4 accidents involving the car in autonomous mode in 2015. Of those 4, 1 could have been avoided, 1 is questionable, and seem to have been 2 unavoidable. That is not quite as impressive a stat. The technology is impressive, but it is not perfect.
